text: What the 2026 IDC MarketScape report reveals about Sophos enterprise endpoint security Cybersecurity vendor Sophos has earned a Leader placement in the IDC MarketScape: Worldwide Modern Endpoint Security for Enterprises 2026 Vendor Assessment (#US54123526, September 2026). The evaluation highlights the platform’s robust up-front protection against web, exploit, and ransomware threat vectors—a capability validated across multiple independent testing programs that significantly lowers analyst workload and alert volumes. The recognition comes at a critical time for enterprise defenders. According to the Sophos AI Security 2026 Report, threat actors are leveraging artificial intelligence to discover vulnerabilities, develop exploits, and execute attacks at unprecedented speed, with high-profile vulnerabilities being weaponized within 24 to 36 hours of public disclosure. This rapidly narrowing window leaves security operations teams with minimal time to apply patches or manually correlate risk signals across disparate systems. Sophos Endpoint addresses this operational pressure by deploying a prevention-first model that executes natively across every process: Deep Learning AI: Identifies and halts both known and previously unseen malware variants, including AI-generated and AI-mutated threats, prior to execution. Default Exploit Mitigations: Activates more than 60 out-of-the-box exploit mitigations to neutralize the underlying techniques attackers use to exploit software vulnerabilities. Operational Efficiency: Delivers enterprise-grade security without requiring complex, manual tuning or adding operational friction for IT teams. “AI is compressing the time between vulnerability discovery and exploitation, and security teams are still grappling with the realities of patching at scale,” said Kyle Falkenhagen, senior vice president of product management at Sophos. “We believe this recognition reflects Sophos’ ability to meet the needs of enterprises operating in increasingly complex, fast-moving threat environments. Organizations need endpoint protection that stops the techniques attackers rely on before they become business-impacting events, and that’s exactly what Sophos Endpoint is built to deliver. As part of Sophos Fusion, that protection extends into a coordinated defense system that acts across the entire environment.” In its vendor analysis, the IDC MarketScape recommended that enterprise decision-makers “consider Sophos when organizations need a unified, open platform with strong third-party integration, native identity threat detection, and automation. SMBs to large enterprises are seeking out-of-the-box, protection-first endpoint security with minimal tuning.” Sophos Endpoint serves as a foundational component within Sophos Fusion, the vendor’s AI-native cybersecurity defense system. Within this framework, endpoint telemetry feeds into a centralized context lake alongside telemetry from other native controls and more than 500 third-party integrations. Through its Synchronized Security mechanism, a threat identified on a single endpoint automatically triggers coordinated containment actions across the wider network infrastructure. Conversely, telemetry gathered from identity systems, firewalls, email channels, and cloud workloads feeds directly back into the endpoint layer to accelerate threat investigation and remediation. The connected security architecture is powered by Sophos X-Ops threat intelligence and real-world incident response telemetry collected across more than 625,000 protected organizations worldwide, allowing security teams to correlate alerts, analyze suspicious behavior, and execute cross-platform threat response from a unified console. #2026 #latest #news #Philippines #Sophos #Technology

Why the Philippines is demanding a shift to multi-year climate adaptation funding As global temperatures threaten to cross critical warming thresholds, the Philippines is urging the international community to abandon short-term, project-based climate financing in favor of predictable, multi-year funding to build permanent, nationally owned systems of resilience. Speaking at the Solutions Dialogue on Financing Adaptation in the Era of Global Overshoot at United Nations Headquarters in New York, Atty. Analiza Rebuelta-Teh, Department of Environment and Natural Resources (DENR) Undersecretary for Finance, Information Systems, Climate Change and Administration, highlighted the urgent need to sustain early warning capabilities so that alerts lead directly to protective action. For climate-vulnerable island nations like the Philippines, “we are already confronting increasingly intense and compounding hazards that threaten lives, livelihoods, food and water security, ecosystems, and economic stability”, Undersecretary Rebuelta-Teh said. The call comes as financial pressure mounts on developing countries. Global adaptation costs for developing nations are projected to reach $310 billion to $365 billion annually by 2035—a burden amplified by widespread debt distress and high capital costs. In the Philippines, delaying action carries a severe economic burden: inaction across eight priority sectors outlined in the National Adaptation Plan (NAP) is estimated to cost the country ₱645 billion every year. “Adaptation cannot remain reactive,” the Undersecretary emphasized. “We need new, additional, predictable, and scaled-up public finance to enable developing countries to respond to growing climate risks at the speed and scale required.” To build sustainable financing for early warning infrastructure, Rebuelta-Teh outlined three priority areas: Treating early warning systems as permanent public infrastructure: Transitioning away from short-term project grants toward multi-year, predictable financing streams. Funding last-mile action: Securing pre-arranged, trigger-based funding alongside local risk data, warning distribution systems, and community preparedness programs to ensure alerts trigger immediate local protection. Financing the “unfunded middle” and securing domestic ownership: Providing resources for continuous operations, system maintenance, data collection, staff training, and technical upgrades, establishing a clear path toward full domestic budget integration. Reinforcing its commitment to global disaster risk management, the Philippines recently formalized its entry as the 71st member of the Coalition for Disaster Resilient Infrastructure (CDRI), becoming only the second Southeast Asian nation to join the international organization. “For the Philippines, our goal is to move from isolated projects to permanent, nationally owned systems of resilience,” Undersecretary Rebuelta-Teh said. “With predictable international support aligned with domestic planning and budgeting, we can ensure that early warnings are not only issued, but translated into timely action that protects lives, livelihoods, and development gains.” #2026 #DENR #latest #news #Philippines

The Archipelago Strategy: How a Philippine University Network Is Blueprinting the Future of Higher Education On a tropical midmorning in Manila, where the relentless hum of traffic along the Pasig River mirrors the rapid cadence of Southeast Asia’s digital economy, a quiet structural revolution is reshaping how the developing world prepares its young for the future of work. Across the Philippine archipelago, some 75 million citizens comprise the working-age population, a demographic dividend that economists have long cited as the nation’s greatest untapped growth engine. Yet inside the lecture halls and executive suites of Manila’s top institutions, a stubborn paradox has persisted for decades: while higher education enrollments have expanded, the gap between academic curricula and the hyper-fluid demands of global industry has widened into a chasm. Enter iPeople, inc. (PSE:IPO), the educational holding vehicle under House of Investments, Inc. (PSE:HI) and the prestigious Yuchengco Group of Companies. Rather than attempting to incrementally overhaul decades-old university syllabi through traditional, sluggish bureaucratic channels, iPeople took a radically pragmatic leap. Through its flagship institutions, most notably Mapúa University, long revered as the country’s premier engineering and technological powerhouse, the group quietly integrated digital microcredentials, generative artificial intelligence skills, and industry certifications directly into its core degree programs. The bold gamble has paid off on a global stage. Out of more than 780 higher education institutions evaluated across the globe, iPeople was named the sole recipient of Coursera’s Global Learning Excellence Award at the platform’s marquee FWD event. The accolade recognizes visionary organizations that have fundamentally dismantled traditional barriers to higher education, proving that an emerging market network can out-innovate legacy institutions in Western economies. “For the iPeople group of institutions, one of the things that we like to do is recognize exemplars,” says Anthony Salcito, Senior Vice President and President of Enterprise at Coursera, sitting down to reflect on the global milestone. “This is a very, very important time in the world of skilling as so many jobs are changing. Reskilling has become an imperative across the 3.7 billion workers in jobs today, and the 75 million Filipinos who are in the working-age labor force need to be reskilled and upskilled continually.” What began in 2019 as a pre-pandemic initiative to expand online course access has evolved into a sophisticated hybrid paradigm. Today, the partnership reaches over 45,000 active learners annually across the iPeople system, with Coursera’s third-party coursework contributing to roughly 20 percent of students’ required academic credits. In an era where artificial intelligence threatens to render traditional four-year degrees obsolete before the ink on a diploma can dry, iPeople’s model offers a compelling blueprint for how higher education can survive and lead the age of automation. https://youtu.be/sGn_W2LGr3E?si=cueh23eGJlXGoLBx The speed of disruption vs. the slow grind of academia To understand why a university network in the Philippines beat out hundreds of global rivals for top learning honors requires examining the acute structural crisis facing global higher education. Historically, university faculty members have served as the ultimate guardians of knowledge. A professor drafts a syllabus, refines it over a decade, and delivers lecture material that remains relatively stable. But the exponential acceleration of software development, cloud computing, and now generative AI has dismantled that cadence. “One of the things that I think universities struggle with is creating a reason why, in many cases, getting faculty to understand how this is going to add value,” Salcito explains with the seasoned authority of a veteran edtech executive. Salcito, who spent more than two decades shaping Microsoft’s worldwide education strategy before executive stints at Nerdy and his eventual arrival at Coursera, understands the friction inherent in university boardrooms. “Faculty members are going to tell you their core mission is to help students get on a path to a career, so they ask, ‘Why do I need Coursera’s help? I’m already doing that every day in my classroom,'” Salcito observes. “The difference is the pace of content and the pace of skills are changing so rapidly that faculty members can’t possibly have the latest and greatest skills that are needed. They don’t have the global perspective on layering those careers and skills into jobs and roles as effectively. The credential signals to employers that students are role-ready.” The World Economic Forum’s recent Future of Jobs Report estimates that 44 percent of workers’ core skills will be disrupted over the next five years, driven primarily by technological breakthroughs. For a developing economy like the Philippines, where the Business Process Outsourcing (BPO) and IT-BPM sectors contribute over $35 billion annually to national GDP and employ over 1.7 million professionals, skill displacement is not an abstract academic exercise. It is an immediate macroeconomic vulnerability. If entry-level white-collar jobs are automated by AI agents, the traditional pipeline elevating young Filipinos into the middle class collapses. By embedding microcredentials directly into standard degree paths, iPeople created a dual-engine degree: theoretical grounding delivered by tenured university faculty, paired with real-time, vendor-certified technical competencies from global tech titans like Google, IBM, and Meta. The geography of AI adoption: A Philippine case study While Western commentators debate the ethics or speculative risks of artificial intelligence, everyday adoption across emerging Asian markets is moving at a breakneck pace. In the Philippines, the appetite for digital upskilling has reached a fever pitch. “We see tremendous demand for AI skills, and it is growing significantly year-over-year in the Philippines,” Salcito reveals. “We have one learner enrolling in an AI course every two minutes in the Philippines. So it’s happening while we’re in this meeting.” This rapid adoption reflects more than basic curiosity about chat interfaces; it represents a fundamental shift in technical literacy. “In general, there’s still lots of folks taking core AI fundamentals content,” Salcito says, “but things are obviously moving to focus on building AI-adjacent work and AI agents, as well as AI in the context of leadership. How do I lead in the context of AI? What decision-making changes are needed?” Crucially, Coursera’s global empirical data reveals a fascinating counter-trend to the narrative that automation simply replaces human labor. The platform’s internal tracking shows that technical proficiency in AI is increasingly tied to foundational soft skills, a relationship formalized in the company’s recent Job Skills Report under the “AI Synergy Index.” Technical AI competencies, such as machine learning, prompt engineering, and agentic AI frameworks, are soaring in demand across regional industries. However, complementary human skills like critical thinking, complex problem-solving, and ethical reasoning are growing just as rapidly alongside them. While automated systems handle execution, industry leadership increasingly demands strategic oversight and holistic decision-making. https://youtu.be/Bpa6LXmr_cc?si=_M1x7XEYM-mTCkjI For Mapúa University and its sister institutions within the iPeople ecosystem, this synergy forms the core of their institutional differentiation. Rather than viewing online learning platforms as competitors or passive libraries, iPeople uses algorithmic skills mapping, leveraging global data points from millions of learners, to help faculty construct clear pathways for students. Instead of wandering through thousands of unstructured video modules, students follow optimized curricula engineered to match explicit job descriptions in the regional and global market. Bridging the hyper-local gap: Project Helix and local context A perennial critique of global edtech platforms in the Global South has been their reliance on Silicon Valley- or Ivy League-centric perspectives. A computer science course taught by a professor at Stanford or an executive at an American cloud provider may offer world-class fundamentals, but it often lacks insight into local regulatory frameworks, regional market dynamics, and cultural workplace nuance. Coursera’s acquisition of marketplace platform Udemy was a strategic move designed to solve this exact problem. By uniting Coursera’s institutional university partnerships with Udemy’s expansive catalog of practitioner-instructors, the enterprise created a global-local feedback loop. “Udemy brings in over 100,000 content creators, and there are well over 500 Filipino content creators, many of whom are very, very popular, not only in the Philippines, but all over the region,” Salcito says. “That enables us to bring people who have deep subject matter expertise, but also local context. That, coupled with all the global providers, is the true benefit of bringing these two platforms together.” To seamlessly operationalize this vast reservoir of content, Coursera is rolling out an AI-native infrastructure platform internally known as CodeName Helix. Project Helix operates by synthesizing global institutional foundations from partners like Yale, Stanford, Microsoft, and Google with the hyper-local context provided by regional creators. Through automated translation, cultural adaptation, and continuous content verification, the platform generates learning pathways that honor regional law and economic realities alongside world-class technical standards. “Helix will enable the capability to bring the content libraries of Coursera and Udemy together,” Salcito reveals. “Whether it’s in the Philippines or in Brazil, it’s not just the language, but the economic issues, the legal dynamics with regard to regulations. All that context will be in the product. It’s hard to do that with Yale University and Microsoft alone, but those local content creators provide that localized specialization.” When pressed on how the platform verifies accuracy and academic rigor among crowdsourced local creators, Salcito points to a dual vetting mechanism: strict initial subject-matter verification combined with real-time peer signals from millions of enterprise learners. “They have to demonstrate deep subject matter expertise to get on the platform, but they are also continuously vetted by the learners themselves. People enrolling in the course, seeing value, seeing results, those ratings directly govern visibility and quality control.” Redefining the diploma: The shift to lifelong learning The structural integration achieved by iPeople raises a broader question about the future of global higher education: Is the hybrid 80/20 model, where 20 percent of degree credits derive from digital platforms, a temporary stepping stone, or the permanent architecture of the modern university? Salcito believes we are witnessing a permanent shift in the social contract between universities, students, and employers. The four-year university degree is no longer a terminal destination; it is an initial launchpad designed to instill habits of continuous skill acquisition. In the legacy higher education model, a student completed a four-year academic degree, entered the workforce, and spent the next four decades experiencing gradual skill decay toward eventual professional obsolescence. Under the hybrid model pioneered by iPeople and Coursera, the core academic degree is augmented with industry microcredentials from day one, establishing a rhythm of continuous upskilling loops that sustain long-term career resiliency. “Higher education is going to be a critical fuel for a changing workplace dynamic,” Salcito emphasizes. “The ideal scenario is that external industry content is seamlessly embedded into the learning journey for students. But in addition to the content, the vital thing universities do with this process is instill a fundamental understanding that learning and development must be continuous throughout a career path.” “The most important skill a student can gain, outside of what they learn in their specific degree program, is that hunger to continue learning going forward,” Salcito continues. “If I take an AI course today and get a certification, that’s not a done situation. Six months from now, there will be new models, new capabilities, and new areas to master. So embedding this experience directly into the university structure signals a massive cultural shift: the degree is not the final outcome. It’s about getting people to build skills continually as they progress through the workforce.” For the Philippine higher education sector, iPeople’s recognition as a global exemplar marks a decisive shift in narrative. Long viewed as an emerging market attempting to catch up with Western academic standards, the country is now demonstrating how agility, institutional partnership, and forward-looking leadership can leapfrog legacy educational infrastructure entirely. As economic pressures force universities worldwide to justify their return on investment to students facing soaring tuition costs, the lesson from Manila is remarkably clear: the universities that thrive in the twenty-first century will not be those that fight the pace of technological change, but those that build the bridge directly to it. #2026 #BUSINESS #Coursera #events #latest #Mapua #news #Philippines #Technology
